invariant_bindings.invariant_text: Every outbound call MUST use min(local_timeout, TimeoutBudget.remaining_ms()) and NEVER the local timeout alone.
The deadline MUST be measured on a monotonic clock and SHALL NOT move backward on wall-clock jumps.
A call issued when remaining_ms is not positive SHALL be refused before any socket I/O begins.
The budget CANNOT be extended inside the request scope; a derived child budget MUST NEVER exceed the parent's deadline. FORBIDDEN to renew without a new request boundary.
The budget SHALL be propagated across task boundaries via the CURRENT_BUDGET context variable and NEVER via thread-local state.

tier_reports.summary: mypy --strict clean; ruff (curated ALL) clean; 1 suppressions all rationale-attached.
LLM judge ≥8/10 on six axes; all five personas understood the docs.

attacks.hypothesis: A downstream httpx client is initialized with a hardcoded timeout=30.0 at module import and never consults TimeoutBudget.remaining_ms(), so a request with 200ms remaining will wait 30s on a slow upstream and outlive its parent deadline.
attacks.input_fixture: set deadline_ns to now+200ms; invoke downstream call via pre-built httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=30.0); upstream sleeps 5s

attacks.hypothesis: If deadline_ns is derived from time.time()*1e9 instead of time.monotonic_ns(), an NTP step backward of 10s while the request is in flight will make remaining_ms() return a falsely-large positive value and the call will outlive the original deadline.
attacks.input_fixture: freeze wall clock, start budget(500ms), step wall clock back 10s mid-flight, call remaining_ms()

attacks.hypothesis: When remaining_ms() returns 0 exactly (boundary), for_call(max_ms) may return 0 and still be passed to socket.connect(timeout=0), which on some platforms means 'blocking forever' rather than 'refuse immediately'.
attacks.input_fixture: deadline_ns = monotonic_ns(); call for_call(1000) then socket.create_connection(addr, timeout=result)

attacks.hypothesis: After deadline has passed by 50ms, remaining_ms() returns -50 and for_call naively does min(max_ms, -50) returning -50, which when cast to httpx timeout raises or is coerced to None=infinite.
attacks.input_fixture: sleep past deadline; invoke for_call(5000); pass to httpx.get(timeout=...)

attacks.hypothesis: A middleware re-enters the scope and calls CURRENT_BUDGET.set(new_budget_with_later_deadline), effectively extending the deadline within the same request, violating the no-extension invariant.
attacks.input_fixture: within request scope: CURRENT_BUDGET.set(TimeoutBudget(deadline_ns=monotonic_ns()+10_000_000_000))

attacks.hypothesis: Code offloads work via loop.run_in_executor or threading.Thread without contextvars.copy_context, so the worker thread sees CURRENT_BUDGET as None and falls back to local_timeout alone.
attacks.input_fixture: async handler schedules blocking job via ThreadPoolExecutor that calls downstream HTTP

attacks.hypothesis: asyncio.ensure_future with a custom loop or using loop.call_soon_threadsafe from another thread drops the contextvar copy, leaving downstream tasks with no budget.
attacks.input_fixture: from thread A: loop.call_soon_threadsafe(lambda: asyncio.create_task(downstream()))

attacks.hypothesis: Passing max_ms=2**63 to for_call causes deadline_ns arithmetic (now + max_ms*1_000_000) to overflow Python-int-to-C-int boundary when handed to select()/epoll, yielding negative timeouts interpreted as immediate or indefinite.
attacks.input_fixture: for_call(2**63); forward result to selectors.DefaultSelector.select(timeout=...)

attacks.hypothesis: If origin/deadline propagates over HTTP via X-Deadline-Ms header and the server trusts it blindly, an attacker replays a stale request with a forged huge deadline to bypass budget enforcement on an internal service.
attacks.input_fixture: curl -H 'X-Deadline-Ms: 999999999' internal-svc/endpoint

attacks.hypothesis: Implementation uses a module-level dict keyed by thread id instead of ContextVar, so two concurrent asyncio tasks on the same thread share/overwrite each other's budget, leading to one request inheriting another's (longer) deadline.
attacks.input_fixture: gather(request_A(deadline=50ms), request_B(deadline=30_000ms)); observe A using B's remaining

attacks.hypothesis: origin='' (empty string) or None bypasses auditing/enforcement middleware that gates on `if budget.origin:` and silently disables deadline checks for this request.
attacks.input_fixture: construct TimeoutBudget(deadline_ns=..., origin='')

attacks.hypothesis: A retry wrapper uses for_call(max_ms) once then retries N times reusing the same max_ms without re-consulting remaining_ms, so total wall time = N*max_ms far exceeding the budget.
attacks.input_fixture: tenacity.retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(5), wait=wait_fixed(2)) around call using for_call(5000)

attacks.hypothesis: origin is populated from user-controlled request header without sanitization and later interpolated into a logged audit string or shell subprocess, enabling log-injection or command injection.
attacks.input_fixture: X-Origin: "foo\n[CRIT] deadline bypassed; rm -rf /"

attacks.hypothesis: remaining_ms() integer-floors 0.4ms to 0, causing for_call to refuse a call that actually has 400 microseconds of budget remaining — but in some impls it returns 1 (ceil), causing I/O to proceed past deadline.
attacks.input_fixture: deadline_ns = monotonic_ns() + 400_000; call remaining_ms()

attacks.hypothesis: remaining_ms() is called, returns a positive value, but the budget expires in the nanoseconds between that read and the value being passed to the socket connect call. The check passes, I/O begins, yet the budget was already exhausted at I/O start — violating the 'refused before any socket I/O begins' invariant under a race window that grows with CPU contention.
attacks.input_fixture:
budget = make_budget(deadline_ns=time.monotonic_ns()+1_000_000)  # 1ms
rm = budget.remaining_ms()  # returns 1
time.sleep(0.002)  # budget now expired
httpx.get(url, timeout=budget.for_call(5000))  # I/O begins with stale positive check

attacks.hypothesis: If the implementation derives deadline_ns from time.time_ns() rather than time.monotonic_ns(), an NTP step-back of even 1 second will cause remaining_ms() to return a value larger than the true remaining budget, allowing calls to proceed past their actual deadline, violating the monotonic-clock invariant.
attacks.input_fixture:
# Simulate NTP step-back
with mock.patch('time.time_ns', side_effect=[1_000_000_000_000, 999_000_000_000]):
    budget = make_budget(ttl_ms=500)
    assert budget.remaining_ms() > 500  # clock went backward, remaining inflated

attacks.hypothesis: If the pre-call guard is implemented as 'remaining_ms() < 0' instead of '<= 0', a budget where remaining_ms() returns exactly 0 will pass the guard and initiate socket I/O with a zero-millisecond timeout, effectively a fire-and-forget with undefined behavior. The invariant says 'not positive' (i.e., <= 0) must be refused.
attacks.input_fixture:
budget = make_budget(deadline_ns=time.monotonic_ns())  # exactly now
assert budget.remaining_ms() == 0
assert budget.expired() == True
# guard: if budget.remaining_ms() < 0: raise  -- misses == 0 case
call_with_budget(budget)  # must NOT reach socket

attacks.hypothesis: asyncio.create_task() copies the current context snapshot at creation time, but if the budget ContextVar is set AFTER the task is spawned (e.g., in middleware that sets it post-dispatch), the task sees CURRENT_BUDGET=None and silently falls back to its local timeout, bypassing propagation entirely.
attacks.input_fixture:
async def handler():
    task = asyncio.create_task(downstream())  # context snapshot taken HERE, budget=None
    CURRENT_BUDGET.set(make_budget(ttl_ms=200))  # set AFTER task creation
    await task  # downstream sees None budget, uses local_timeout=5000ms alone

attacks.hypothesis: Code running in loop.run_in_executor() (a ThreadPoolExecutor) does NOT inherit ContextVar values unless contextvars.copy_context().run() is used explicitly. A blocking DB call inside an executor will read CURRENT_BUDGET as None and apply only its own local timeout, violating the propagation invariant.
attacks.input_fixture:
async def fetch_from_db():
    CURRENT_BUDGET.set(make_budget(ttl_ms=300))
    result = await asyncio.get_event_loop().run_in_executor(
        None, blocking_db_query  # ContextVar NOT propagated to thread
    )
    # blocking_db_query reads CURRENT_BUDGET.get() => None

attacks.hypothesis: If deadline_ns is a plain mutable attribute (not a read-only property), any code within the request scope can reassign it to extend the deadline, violating the 'budget CANNOT be extended inside the request scope' invariant. A middleware or interceptor could silently do this as an optimization.
attacks.input_fixture:
budget = make_budget(ttl_ms=100)
CURRENT_BUDGET.set(budget)
# Attacker-controlled middleware:
budget.deadline_ns = time.monotonic_ns() + 60_000_000_000  # extend by 60s
assert budget.remaining_ms() > 59_000  # invariant violated

attacks.hypothesis: When N parallel downstream calls each invoke for_call(max_ms), they all receive min(local_max, remaining_ms()) independently. The budget does not partition itself across fans-out — each branch gets the full remaining budget. A request with 1000ms remaining can fan out to 100 parallel calls each with 1000ms, amplifying wall-clock exposure by 100x beyond intent.

When CURRENT_BUDGET.get() returns None (budget was never set, e.g., an internal cron job calls a shared utility), the outbound call helper may fall back to using only the local_timeout parameter. This means the invariant 'NEVER use local timeout alone' is silently violated for any code path where the budget was not injected.
attacks.input_fixture:
# No budget set — simulates cron/internal call path
assert CURRENT_BUDGET.get() is None
# If helper does: timeout = budget.remaining_ms() if budget else local_timeout
httpx.get(url, timeout=30)  # local timeout used alone, invariant broken

attacks.hypothesis: A budget object from a completed request (deadline already expired) is stored in a cache or object pool and reused for a new request without resetting the deadline_ns. The new request inherits an already-expired budget, causing all calls to be refused immediately, or if the guard is wrong, proceeds with a negative remaining_ms passed to timeout.
attacks.input_fixture:
budget = make_budget(ttl_ms=100)
time.sleep(0.2)  # budget expires
request_pool.put(budget)  # pooled for reuse

# New request
new_budget = request_pool.get()  # stale, expired
CURRENT_BUDGET.set(new_budget)
assert new_budget.remaining_ms() < 0  # all calls immediately refused

attacks.hypothesis: remaining_ms() converts monotonic nanoseconds to milliseconds via integer division (ns // 1_000_000). For a budget with 999_999 ns remaining (~0.999ms), this returns 0, causing a premature refusal. Conversely, if rounded up (math.ceil), 1ns remaining returns 1ms, allowing a call that will certainly timeout. Either truncation or ceiling creates a systematic boundary error.
attacks.input_fixture:
budget = make_budget(deadline_ns=time.monotonic_ns() + 999_999)  # 0.999ms
assert budget.remaining_ms() == 0  # truncation: premature refusal
# OR
assert budget.remaining_ms() == 1  # ceiling: allows call with ~0ms true budget

attacks.hypothesis: If deadline_ns is set with a very large TTL (e.g., ttl_ms=2**53 passed by a misconfigured caller), adding it to time.monotonic_ns() can overflow a 64-bit signed integer in Python-native implementations or in Rust/C extensions that serialize to i64. The overflowed deadline wraps to a past timestamp, making remaining_ms() return a large negative number and refusing all calls immediately.
attacks.input_fixture:
import sys
big_ttl_ms = sys.maxsize  # 9223372036854775807
big_ttl_ns = big_ttl_ms * 1_000_000  # overflows int64 in C extensions
budget = make_budget(ttl_ms=big_ttl_ms)
assert budget.deadline_ns > 0  # may be negative after overflow

attacks.hypothesis: The 'origin' field is a free-form string set by the caller and propagated to distributed traces, structured logs, and audit records. An attacker controlling an inbound header (e.g., X-Request-Origin) can inject newline characters or JSON-breaking sequences into origin, causing log forging, corrupted trace spans, or SIEM alert suppression if the downstream observability pipeline does not sanitize it.
attacks.input_fixture:
malicious_origin = 'svc-A\n{"level":"INFO","msg":"auth_ok","user":"admin"}'
budget = make_budget(ttl_ms=500, origin=malicious_origin)
# Structured logger emits: {"origin": "svc-A\n{...forged line...}"}
# Log parsers split on newline, treating forged JSON as a separate log entry

attacks.hypothesis: for_call(max_ms=-1) is called by a misconfigured caller. If the implementation computes min(remaining_ms(), max_ms) and remaining_ms() is positive, the result is -1, which is then passed as a timeout to an HTTP client. Most clients interpret negative timeouts as 'infinite' or raise an error after I/O has already begun, violating the pre-I/O refusal invariant.
attacks.input_fixture:
budget = make_budget(ttl_ms=1000)
timeout = budget.for_call(max_ms=-1)  # min(1000, -1) = -1
httpx.get(url, timeout=timeout)  # httpx treats -1 as infinite timeout

attacks.hypothesis: Implementation uses local_timeout directly instead of min(local_timeout, remaining_ms), allowing calls to exceed the global deadline.
attacks.input_fixture: TimeoutBudget(deadline_ns=1000ms ago, remaining_ms=0) + local_timeout=5000ms → socket call proceeds instead of rejecting

attacks.hypothesis: Integer overflow in remaining_ms calculation when deadline_ns is very large, returning negative value interpreted as large timeout.
attacks.input_fixture: deadline_ns=2^63-1, current_time=now() → remaining_ms wraps to negative, passed to min() as large positive

attacks.hypothesis: Deadline calculated using wall-clock time instead of monotonic clock, causing backward jump when system time adjusts (NTP, daylight savings).
attacks.input_fixture: System time jumps backward 1 hour → deadline_ns recalculated with old reference, effective timeout extends backward in real time.

attacks.hypothesis: No guard against negative remaining_ms when clock skew or monotonic clock reset occurs, allowing socket calls with inverted deadline.
attacks.input_fixture: remaining_ms = -500 (clock went backward) → not validated before socket I/O, connection hangs with invalid timeout.

attacks.hypothesis: Race condition where remaining_ms is checked as positive, but by the time socket I/O starts, budget has expired in another thread.
attacks.input_fixture: Thread A: check remaining_ms > 0 (true), context switch, Thread B: expire budget, Thread A: issue socket call with expired budget

attacks.hypothesis: TimeoutBudget object is mutable; caller extends deadline_ns directly without new request boundary, breaking propagation contract.
attacks.input_fixture: budget.deadline_ns += 10_000_000_000 (add 10 more seconds) inside request handler, violates no-extension invariant

attacks.hypothesis: Async sibling tasks don't inherit ContextVar correctly when spawned without context copy, one task sees another's budget.
attacks.input_fixture: create_task(handler_b()) without copying context from handler_a → budget from handler_a leaks or handler_b loses budget entirely

attacks.hypothesis: New thread spawned without setting ContextVar, child thread has no budget context even though parent does.
attacks.input_fixture: threading.Thread(target=worker).start() where worker calls socket with budget from parent → ContextVar returns None, no timeout enforced

attacks.hypothesis: Old budget from previous request (deadline already passed) is reused in a new request due to improper context reset.
attacks.input_fixture: Request A ends with budget expired, Request B reuses same context without clearing ContextVar → Request B inherits dead budget

attacks.hypothesis: remaining_ms at exact boundary (zero) allows marginal socket call when specification requires refusal before any I/O.
attacks.input_fixture: remaining_ms checks deadline is exactly 0, caller issues socket with zero timeout instead of immediate rejection

attacks.hypothesis: When ContextVar returns None (budget not set), implementation falls back to infinite timeout instead of requiring explicit budget.
attacks.input_fixture: Worker function called without ContextVar.set() → remaining_ms() returns None, fallback to 300s local timeout, no deadline enforced

attacks.hypothesis: Multiple concurrent requests share same TimeoutBudget object via shallow copy, modifications in one request affect others.
attacks.input_fixture: Request A and B both reference same budget object in context, Request A modifies origin field, Request B sees contaminated budget

axes.rationale: Protocol matches catalog api_signature verbatim (deadline_ns, origin, remaining_ms, for_call, expired) and CURRENT_BUDGET ContextVar is exposed. Monotonic clock only, immutable post-init, derive enforces child ≤ parent. Minor: Protocol attributes declared at class level without defaults — acceptable for runtime_checkable.

All five invariants covered with enforcement paths: for_call (TB-01/03), monotonic_ns (TB-02), __setattr__ freeze + derive cap (TB-04), bind/current via ContextVar (TB-05). Header codec and GuardedCall provide extension surface. from_ms root factory included.

Dedicated taxonomy: TimeoutBudgetInvariantError base + TimeoutBudgetExpired subclass for short-circuit distinction. Every raise cites the invariant ID, includes offending value and context (origin, types). noqa on N818 documents the catalog-visible naming choice.

Protocol-based surface, contextvars propagation (async-safe), symmetric DeadlineHeaderCodec for transport hops, GuardedCall as test-double transport. derive enables hierarchical composition. Zero import-time I/O. __all__ is explicit.

Immutable dataclass-like via __slots__ + frozen guard, monotonic-only clock, lock-guarded refusal counter in GuardedCall, lazy/no I/O at import. Clear SRE signals documented in spec (refusals metric, for_call histogram). No observability hooks wired in-module but that's the adopter's job per extension contract.

Protocol signature matches catalog byte-for-byte; CURRENT_BUDGET name and default align; invariants 01–05 each mapped to concrete enforcement with IDs cited in docstrings and error messages. Namespace (resiliency) and maturity (battle_tested) reflected in spec doc. Consumption example mirrors catalog.

friction_points: contextvars.ContextVar vs thread-local distinction is introduced without explaining what a ContextVar is or why it matters for async code
The invariant table lists rules (TB_INV_01–05) before any usage example, so a reader doesn't yet know what 'outbound call' or 'dispatch' means in this codebase
DeadlineHeaderCodec and GuardedCall are named in the API surface but have no usage snippet — their role is only inferable from the invariant-binding paragraph
reviews.rewrite_suggestion: Move the usage example to the top of the API surface section and annotate each line (e.g., '# propagates via asyncio task automatically'). Add one sentence defining ContextVar: 'a Python stdlib slot that asyncio copies into every new task so the budget follows your coroutines without extra plumbing.' Add a two-line GuardedCall snippet next to its definition.

friction_points: from_ms creates a root budget but the underlying clock source (time.monotonic_ns, perf_counter?) is not stated — critical for knowing whether cross-process deadline math is valid
GuardedCall's interface (constructor signature, what 'records each dispatch's effective timeout' means in practice) is described in prose but never shown as code
derive(child_max_ms) nesting depth: no guidance on whether a 10-hop deep call tree accumulates GC pressure or whether derived budgets share the parent's monotonic reference point
reviews.rewrite_suggestion: Add a 'Internals' subsection: state the clock call, show that derive() stores a reference to the root deadline (not a copy), and note that nesting is O(1) in memory. Show GuardedCall.__init__ and .dispatches property signatures in the API surface table.

friction_points: origin is described as 'free-form label used for logging' but no sanitization contract is stated — a hostile caller can inject newlines or ANSI escapes into structured logs
DeadlineHeaderCodec.decode maximum accepted value is unspecified — an attacker sending X-Deadline-Ms: 2^63 cannot widen the budget but may cause integer overflow or allocation in the decoder
No mention of what decode raises on non-integer, negative, or absent header values — callers need to know whether to expect ValueError, TimeoutBudgetExpired, or a silent zero
reviews.rewrite_suggestion: Add a 'Input validation' paragraph to the Security section: specify origin is truncated to N chars and stripped of control characters before emission; state the accepted numeric range for the header (e.g., 1–3_600_000 ms) and that values outside it raise TimeoutBudgetExpired; enumerate the three error cases for decode.

friction_points: Metric names (timeout.budget.refusals, timeout.budget.for_call) are listed without label schemas — oncall cannot write a Prometheus alert without knowing the cardinality (service, endpoint, reason labels?)
No guidance on what sets total_ms at ingress: is it a config value, an SLO file, a per-route annotation? SREs need to know where to tune the knob during an incident
No alert threshold or runbook pointer for the 'sustained rise in refusals' symptom — the docs diagnose the signal but leave the response procedure entirely implicit
reviews.rewrite_suggestion: Add an 'Observability reference' table: metric name, type (counter/histogram), and labels. Add a 'Configuration' entry pointing to the ingress adapter config key. Add a one-paragraph runbook stub: 'If timeout.budget.refusals{reason=expired} rises >5% over 5 min, check the for_call histogram for the degraded hop, then inspect upstream p99 latency.'

friction_points: 'Zombie work' and 'stampede' are engineering idioms with no translated customer impact — a PM cannot connect these to an SLA metric or user-visible error rate

The 'when NOT to use' section lists streams and retries but doesn't explain the business consequence of misapplying it (e.g., 'mis-applying to a streaming endpoint will cancel the user's download mid-flight')
No success metric or adoption signal: how does a team know TimeoutBudget is working? The docs are silent on what a healthy vs degraded budget profile looks like at the product level
reviews.rewrite_suggestion: Prepend a 'Business case' paragraph: 'Without deadline propagation, one slow database shard can cause every in-flight request to queue behind it, turning a P99 spike into a full outage. TimeoutBudget stops the cascade at source and makes tail-latency budget visible per hop.' Add a 'You'll know it's working when' line: 'P99 error rate from downstream timeouts drops and timeout.budget.for_call median stays above your hop SLA.'
